96 Plus, more thoughts on bond funds and leveraged ETFs   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Jason Zweig   October: A Time for Investors to Reap…and Sow   Plus, more thoughts on bond funds and leveraged ETFs     The Limbourg brothers and/or Barthélemy van Eyck, "October," from the Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry (begun ca. 1412) MUSÉE CONDÉ, CHANTILLY, VIA WIKIMEDIA COMMONS   Fellow investors,

   It’s almost October. In the northern hemisphere, October has long been a time for reaping—but also for sowing.

   Yes, in 1987 the stock market crashed on Oct. 19, falling more than 20% in a single day . Over the five days ended Oct. 10, 2008, as the global financial crisis intensified, U.S. stocks lost 18% , the worst week then on record. The panic of 1907, which devastated the U.S. banking system, also erupted in October. Some researchers have even argued for a “ Halloween indicator, ” which steers clear of stocks until after Oct. 31.

   And many investors, in my experience, worry that October is cursed by the market gods .

   Well, then, so is January, when the horrific bear market of 1973-74 began, initiating a 48% wipeout. So is February, when the 22% swoon of 1966 started—and the pandemic panic of 2020. So is March, which kicked off the beginning of the disastrous bear market of 2000-02, when tech stocks fell by about 80%—and the second-worst market downdraft on record, from 1937 to 1942, when the stock market lost 60%. So is April, which in 2011 was the start of a 19% drop that ended at the beginning of October.

   I could go on and on, but Mark Twain said it better than I can:

   OCTOBER: This is one of the peculiarly dangerous months to speculate in stocks in. The others are July, January, September, April, November, May, March, June, December, August, and February. 

   Markets could crash this month, of course—but not because it happens to be October.

   Look at the image above. People six centuries ago, in some ways, thought about the calendar more wisely than we do. The land has been harvested—stripped bare, in fact—but that means it’s also time to plant the winter wheat.

   One man rides a draft horse dragging a wooden harrow, weighted down by a boulder, to break up the soil. Another, in a blue tunic that echoes the sky, scatters wheat seeds in the new furrows. Both are moving on, heading outside our field of vision; soon they’ll be gone, symbolizing the continuity of space and time.

   In the field behind them, a scarecrow in the form of an archer, along with rags fluttering from lines of string, are meant to keep birds from scavenging the newly planted seeds. But, in the foreground, magpies and crows are already swarming to peck at the soil. (Note that they ignore the white sack brimming with seeds at the center; like speculators, they go where the action is, not where the bulk of the wealth can be found!)

   Then, as now, sowing took forethought, discipline and attention to detail. As this spectacular painting shows, even while others are harvesting, you can be planting.

   This is an edition of the Intelligent Investor newsletter, where Jason Zweig writes twice monthly about investment strategy and how to think about money. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       The Incredible Market-Beating Bond Fund: It’s Everywhere!   “If you ain’t cheatin’, you ain’t tryin’” is a popular saying among professional athletes. It often implies bending the rules, or stretching them to the limit, rather than breaking them.

   Investors should be aware that many bond-fund managers may have the same mindset.

   My last column, “ Don’t Fall for Bond Funds That Say They’re Beating the Market ,” looked at the remarkable number of actively managed bond funds that are outperforming the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index, or “the Agg,” a standard benchmark for bond portfolios. Roughly two-thirds of stock funds can’t beat the market, but three-quarters of bond funds can—or so it seems.

   As I pointed out, that’s because the Agg consists mostly of Treasury bonds and entirely of investment-grade bonds, while the typical active bond fund makes plenty of riskier bets.

   Finance professor Caitlin Dannhauser of Villanova University emailed me to share an unpublished research paper that shows just how widespread the problem is. As she told me, “[Many] claims of benchmark outperformance disappear when funds are matched to benchmarks that better represent their risk exposure.”

   By mid-2024, all bond funds had to comply with a Securities and Exchange Commission rule requiring them to display a “broad-based” index in performance comparisons. Look what happened:

         By the end of 2024, points out Dannhauser’s co-author Michael Young, a leading corporate bond index had outperformed the Agg by about 10% over the prior 10 years. So an active corporate-bond fund would look a lot better by comparing itself to the Agg instead of to a corporate index.

   In fact, of the more than 1,000 bond funds Dannhauser and colleagues looked at, nearly 200 added the Agg as a benchmark in 2024—10 times more than in earlier years. On average, between 2010 and 2024, active bond funds beat their reported benchmark by an annualized average of 0.74% over three-year periods. When Dannhauser’s research team used benchmarks reflecting what the funds actually invested in, the average active bond fund underperformed by 0.43% annually.

   “A fund’s benchmark should give you a sense of the risk framework the manager’s going to invest in,” says Mary Ellen Stanek, a veteran fixed-income investor and president of the Baird group of bond funds.

   That’s for sure. If a bond fund owns a boatload of bank loans, business-development companies, emerging-market debt and junk bonds—risky assets that aren’t even included in the Agg—and its performance reporting says it’s outperforming the Agg, the fund is not exactly cheating. But it’s definitely trying too hard.

       Leveraged ETFs for the Long Run?   In the last issue , I looked at the question of whether you can reliably earn higher returns with leveraged ETFs if you just hold them long enough (the topic of my recent column, “ You’re Not Tough Enough to Earn These Huge Returns .” I concluded that you might, if you were incredibly lucky.

   That’s important to remember, because most leveraged ETFs have short track records that don’t include the bear markets of 2008-09 or 2000-02. When the water is smooth, of course you’ll come out ahead in a little speedboat!

   In the rougher waters of the longer term, leverage can hurt badly. I pointed out that a leveraged mutual fund, UltraNasdaq-100 ProFund, that’s a precursor to the popular leveraged Nasdaq-100 ETF, ProShares’ TQQQ, has been around since 1997. Cumulatively, it has underperformed the unleveraged Nasdaq-100.

   Michael Sapir, CEO of ProShares and ProFunds, emailed me to say that “when you’re young, have a long-time horizon, and can take more risk, incorporating leverage in your portfolio can make a lot of sense.”

   The key word there is can. 

   Sapir says his research team simulated how an investor in several leveraged ETFs would have performed relative to an unleveraged index over all rolling 10-year periods and found these results:

     Simulated long-term performance of leveraged funds PROSHARES   The “Hit Ratio” is the percentage of 10-year periods in which the fund beat the unleveraged index. But — and this is a big but, so big that it calls for a ”butt” emoji (‿ˠ‿) — those are simulated results. On the first two funds, ProShares didn’t use their actual expense ratios at the time; it retroactively applied the far lower expense ratios of its equivalent ETFs today. And those two are the only funds in the table whose track records include both the bear market of 2000-02 and 2008-09.

   Finally, to earn that kind of outperformance over 10-year periods, you would have had to survive numerous periods where you’d have lost nearly all your money.

   All investors need at least some luck. Long-term investors in leveraged funds need lots of luck and an almost superhuman tolerance for pain.

     Soga Shōhaku, "Lions at the Stone Bridge of Mount Tiantai" (1779) METROPOLITAN MUSEUM OF ART   In this masterpiece of Japanese painting, Shōhaku visualizes his version of an old Chinese legend. Young lions swarm near a natural stone bridge that crosses a gorge said to be nearly 10 miles deep. A lioness dares her cubs to climb through the mists and scale the slippery cliffs all the way to the top, where she hurls them back down into the chasm. It is her way of culling the weaklings; she will care only for the cubs that survive the fall and clamber back up to the bridge. Anyone hoping to prosper by holding a leveraged ETF for the long run should ponder Shōhaku’s lions tumbling into the depths of the gorge and the long, treacherous path back to the top.

   Be well and invest well,

   Jason
